It is not. He's right. There's a lot in that sentence, and there are a lot of construction companies going out backwards thanks to the policies of this failed Labor government. On the capacity of builders to deliver the homes Australians need, how many homes was it that this Labor government said they were going to build? Was it a million? Then they changed the figure. The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2026-06-24.112.1) to read the bill for a second time. In other words, they voted in favour of a motion to agree with the main idea of the bill and can now discuss it in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2526/26bd069), which is a document prepared by the parliamentary library: > *The Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026 (the Bill) would amend the Fair Work Act 2009 (FW Act) and related legislation to effect industrial relations changes. The key measures are:* > > * *Expanding powers of the Fair Work Commission (FWC) to deal with applications.* > * *Allowing the Commonwealth to preference employers with enterprise agreements for procurement and grants, and for other contractual purposes.* > > *Some changes to the FWC’s powers would respond to the Federal Court decision in Coles Supply Chain Pty Ltd v Milford [2020] FCAFC 152 , so that the FWC is no longer required to determine whether a disputed dismissal actually occurred before conferencing or conciliation.* > > *Other changes to the FWC’s powers would mean that the FWC could make vexatious proceeding orders, dismiss a wider range of matters, determine certain matters without hearings, and allow the FWC President to delegate more powers.* > > *Limited exceptions to the prohibition of adverse action, coercion and discrimination under the FW Act would be made to allow the Commonwealth to preference employers with enterprise agreements in procurement, grant, and other contractual activities. This aspect of the Bill has attracted the most stakeholder comment.* > > *At the time of writing, the Bill had not been referred to or reported on by any parliamentary committees.*

This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed, replacing the current discount system.
The package would introduce a tax floor on gains and update the method for calculating taxable profit to reflect inflation.
The new rules would start on 1 July 2027 and would apply to future gains on assets bought before that date, with exceptions for some housing and small businesses.
Replace the 50% capital gains discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with an indexation system for the cost base.
Create a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules to gains from 1 July 2027, including those on assets bought before that date, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts, partnerships, and some income support recipients who make capital gains.

Australia's small businesses are shutting at a disturbing rate: 40,000 microbusinesses lost in four years as wages that they have to pay go up. Admittedly, the workers are getting less bang for their buck, but tax reforms and calls for a three-day week just mount and small business is doing it so very tough. What I fear is that those opposite don't understand or appreciate the hardships of small business because in many cases they have not run one. They've run picket lines out in front of them and they've run them into the ground, but they haven't actually run a small business to save themselves, and they don't understand and appreciate the complexities facing the operators of those many, many small businesses. I ran one for nearly a decade, with a couple of others, and it's tough. Often you take home less pay yourself than you are in fact paying your employees, your workers. As to workers, yes, we saw the independent commission this week give a wage rise to Australia's lowest paid workers—bearing in mind Australia has one of the highest minimum wages anywhere. But I say to those workers: do not be fooled, because once you take away the power bills, the rent or mortgage costs, the grocery bills and the fuel costs, you're taking home less. Monique Ryan While we're making generational changes to Australia's capital gains tax system, we need to ensure that wholesale reforms don't come at the expense of clear modernisations. The thresholds for small businesses claiming capital gains tax exemptions is such an area of clear modernisation. The existing CGT small-business concession regime, the SBC regime, provides a sliding scale of concessional tax treatment to business owners when they sell their businesses. That regime is preserved by this budget. Under the current Income Tax Act 1997, in order to qualify for the regime, small businesses must have either an aggregated turnover of less than $2 million or combined net assets of less than $6 million. Those thresholds have been unchanged for almost 20 years. The maximum net asset value test was first introduced in 1999, with the Howard government's discount. At that time, the threshold was $5 million for small businesses. That was lifted to $6 million in 2007. The $2 million annual turnover level has also been static since 2007

Anthony Albanese I move: That the amendments be agreed to. Our Labor government is delivering real change to make a real difference—real change built on Australian values: fairness, aspiration and opportunity for all. A $250 tax cut for working Australians, a $1,000 instant tax deduction and a fair crack for first home buyers—these reforms are for young Australians who have been locked out of the housing market for too long, but they're also for their parents and grandparents who want to see the next generation have the opportunity and security of a roof over their head. These reforms are also about rebalancing our tax system and better aligning income from work compared to income derived from assets. Overwhelmingly, most Australians have nothing to sell but their time and nothing to give but their hard work. That is how most Australians earn their income. They work their guts out every day to provide for their families and put food on the table, and for too long the economy has not been working for them. Moved the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, proposing worker tax relief, a $1,000 instant deduction, first-home ownership measures, indexed capital gains taxation and limits on negative gearing for existing residential properties.

Moved that two tax reform bills be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics, arguing that rushed legislation required scrutiny of effects on housing, young people, small businesses, startups, productivity and fairness.

Moved to vary sitting arrangements on 2 and 3 June 2026 to prioritise taxation bills, then moved that debate on two tax reform bills not conclude until every government member had spoken; the motions were agreed to with an absolute majority.
Moved to allow two taxation bills to be debated together and moved that the question be put; the question on the motion was then before the House.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for an advisory report by 30 December 2026, then moved that government business order No. 2 be called on immediately.

Supported tax reform bills that would replace the capital gains tax concession with cost-base indexation from 1 July 2027, limit negative gearing on later-purchased rental properties to new homes, introduce a $250 working Australian tax offset and create a $1,000 instant deduction, arguing the changes would improve fairness and housing affordability.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so debate on the tax reform bills would not conclude until every government member had spoken, then moved that the question be put and later that debate be adjourned, while arguing members should be accountable for the budget's measures.

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Economics for consideration and an advisory report by 30 December 2026.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so specified amendments and remaining stages of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 could be grouped, debated briefly, and put to immediate questions, then moved that the question be put.

Argued that the tax reform bills contain welcome measures on property concessions but require fuller scrutiny, and foreshadowed amendments to split the bill, clarify startup and employee equity protections, limit ministerial powers, protect grandfathered concessions, exempt testamentary trusts, add income protections and reinvest revenue in social and affordable housing; other contributions disputed the bills' effects and supported or opposed them.

Moved procedural motions setting the Senate's hours, business sequence and voting limits for 23 to 29 June 2026, including expedited consideration of tax, appropriation, secrecy, workplace-relations and other bills; then argued that the agreed tax reforms would damage home saving, business growth and aspiration, promising their repeal under a future coalition government.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 and Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing they would reduce investment, business formation and housing opportunities, and criticised proposed exemptions that would require bureaucrats to determine which businesses are innovative.

Moved opposition amendments to remove the capital gains tax and negative gearing schedules from the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026, arguing the package would raise taxes, increase compliance costs and harm housing, investment and businesses; the government said those measures funded tax offsets and rebalanced taxation, before the committee reported progress.

Reported and explained government amendments to the tax reform bills, including raising the active-asset concession threshold from $2 million to $10 million, exempting specified income-support recipients from the minimum capital-gains tax, and removing or narrowing ministerial powers; questions and answers addressed projected revenue, compliance costs and classic-car treatment.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026
This bill is part of a package that would change how capital gains are taxed in Australia.
The package would replace the current 50% capital gains tax discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with a system that adjusts the cost base for inflation, so only real gains are taxed.

It would also introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains from 1 July 2027, with an exemption for some income support recipients, while keeping the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Replace the 50% capital gains tax discount with cost base indexation for individuals, trusts and partnerships.
Introduce a 30% minimum tax on capital gains, exempting certain income support recipients.
Apply the new rules prospectively from 1 July 2027, including to gains on pre-CGT assets, while retaining the discount for new and affordable housing and existing small business concessions.
Individuals, trusts and partnerships that make capital gains.

The bill would permanently enshrine ASIO's compulsory questioning powers in law instead of letting them expire.

People charged with a related offence that is unresolved or imminent could only be questioned before a retired judge serving as a prescribed authority.
Makes the compulsory questioning framework permanent by removing its sunset provision.
Expands the scope of adult compulsory questioning warrants to cover new security threats defined in the ASIO Act.
Amends rules for the appointment and termination of prescribed authorities to strengthen their independence and impartiality.
Adds a new reporting requirement for conduct under a compulsory questioning warrant.
Introduces a safeguard requiring questioning of a person with an unresolved or imminent related charge to happen only before a retired judge.
ASIO, prescribed authorities, people subject to compulsory questioning warrants, and the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

Moved the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, which would make ASIO's compulsory questioning powers permanent, expand adult questioning warrants to additional security matters, strengthen safeguards and reporting requirements, and permit a further review three years after commencement; debate was adjourned.

Declared that, unless otherwise ordered, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025 stood referred to the Federation Chamber after the second-reading debate was adjourned.

Supported the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, arguing that compulsory questioning powers should become permanent, cover additional national security threats and operate with strengthened oversight, reporting and safeguards; noted the powers had been used only 20 times in more than 22 years.

Debated the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, which would make compulsory questioning powers permanent, expand eligible matters and strengthen safeguards and oversight; amendments concerning children were proposed, opposition was stated, and the second-reading question remained unresolved.

Moved bills to make ASIO's compulsory questioning powers permanent and broaden their application while strengthening safeguards and oversight, expand National Immunisation Program access to passive immunological products, and make technical social security and veterans' affairs amendments ahead of 1 July 2026.

Argued that compulsory questioning powers remain important for national security but require strong oversight. Supported expanding the matters covered by warrants, subject to retaining a three-year sunset clause; another speaker opposed making the powers permanent, citing concerns about children, legal representation and extraordinary state powers.

Reaffirmed opposition to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, reading constituent objections to its expanded compulsory questioning powers and citing concerns from the Law Council and the Australian Human Rights Commission, while renewing calls for a national human rights act; the government proposed amendments adding a sunset clause and a two-year statutory review of the new powers.

As President, put questions on a series of amendments to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025 from the government, the Australian Greens, the United Australia Party, One Nation and Senator David Pocock, covering sunset dates for questioning powers, judicial preference for prescribed authorities, lawyers' rights during ASIO questioning and repeal of minor (under-18) questioning warrants, before the bill passed its remaining stages.

Moved an amendment to the Veterans' Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures No. 2) Bill seeking removal of references to notification of the Chief of the Defence Force, citing privacy and access to care; supported the bill's transition to a single framework operating from 1 July 2026 and called for a Senate inquiry.

Argued that the coalition would not oppose the Health Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures No. 1) Bill 2025's technical health-system changes but would seek further scrutiny, while criticising the government's Medicare record; the debate was interrupted before the member completed speaking.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Refining and Improving Our Tax System) Bill 2023

The coalition supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Refining and Improving Our Tax System) Bill 2023 but argued Labor broke promises on franking credits, superannuation taxes and unrealised capital gains, noting $550 billion in tax receipts for 2021–22 and claiming independent research shows 500,000 Australians would be hit by the super tax by retirement.

The government’s mismanagement of the Financial Accountability Regime bills, including a deal with the Greens that was later reversed, delayed their passage, and it broke promises on tax and superannuation, such as doubling super taxes and taxing unrealised capital gains, while the Levy review on financial advice remains unanswered.

The coalition opposes schedules 4 and 5 of the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill, which limit franking credits in share buybacks and capital raisings, breaking Labor’s pre-election promise not to change franking credits; the coalition will move amendments to remove those schedules and will not support the bill if they are kept. The measures are estimated to raise $600 million over five years, mostly from Australians over 75.
